title: Past Simple vs. Present Perfect II — More Practice
subtitle: Extra practice with trickier cases: for/since, questions, and mixed contexts.
objectives: Use "for" and "since" correctly with the present perfect
Ask questions correctly in both tenses
Handle mixed conversations where both tenses appear together

content.intro: Now that you know the basic rule, let's handle the trickier real-life cases — especially "for"/"since", and conversations that naturally move between both tenses.

rules.heading: For vs. since
rules.body:
• for + a period of time: for three years, for two weeks, for a long time
  • since + a starting point: since 2020, since Monday, since I was a child

Both are common with the present perfect: I have lived here for five years. / I have lived here since 2019.

rules.heading: Mixed conversations
rules.body: A conversation often starts with the present perfect ("Have you ever...?") and then switches to the simple past once a specific time is mentioned: "Have you been to Rome?" "Yes, I went there in 2018."

examples: I have lived here for five years.
Have you ever been to Rome? — Yes, I went there in 2018.
How long have you known her? — I've known her since college.
She hasn't called me since last week.
Did you call her yesterday? — No, but I have already texted her.

commonMistakes.wrong: I have lived here since five years.
commonMistakes.right: I have lived here for five years.
commonMistakes.why: "Since" needs a starting point (a date/moment), not a length of time — use "for" with a duration.
"2019" is a starting point — use "since," not "for."

commonMistakes.wrong: Yes, I have been there in 2018.
commonMistakes.why: Once you name a specific finished time (2018), switch to the simple past, even mid-conversation.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with for or since.

items.prompt: I have worked here ___ three years.
They have been married ___ ten years.
"Have you ever visited Rome?" "Yes, I ___ there in 2018."
items.explanation: Once a specific time is named, switch to the simple past.
"How long" with an ongoing state up to now needs the present perfect.

items.incorrect: I have lived here since five years.
answer: I have lived here for five years.
items.explanation: "Since" needs a starting point, not a duration — use "for."

items.incorrect: Yes, I have visited Rome in 2018.
items.explanation: A named specific time needs the simple past, not the present perfect.

summary: For + a duration; since + a starting point.
Conversations often start with the present perfect and switch to the simple past once a specific time is mentioned.
Once you name a specific finished moment, don't go back to the present perfect for the same event.
